comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to cost or data ownership concerns. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch from Jira to Plane to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid service, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to retain full ownership of their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, while Jira offers a more user-friendly onboarding process.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large, complex projects, while Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with Git: Plane offers native integration with Git, while Jira requires a third-party add-on.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Jira
* Pros:
  + User-friendly interface
  + Robust feature set
  + Large community of users and developers
  + Integrates with many third-party tools
  + Offers excellent customer support
* Cons:
  + Expensive, especially for large teams
  + Data stored on Jira's servers, which may be a concern for some teams
  + Limited customization options
  + Can be overwhelming for small teams or simple projects
  + Requires a significant investment of time to fully utilize its features
### Plane
* Pros:
  + Free and self-hosted, giving teams full control over their data
  + Highly customizable
  + Integrates well with Git and other development tools
  + Offers a high degree of flexibility and scalability
  + Has a strong focus on security and data ownership
* Cons:
  + Requires technical expertise to set up and configure
  + Limited user-friendly features and interface
  + May require additional development to integrate with certain tools
  + Limited customer support compared to Jira
  + May not be suitable for very large or complex projects

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large, complex projects that require a robust feature set and excellent customer support. It is also a good option for teams who are already familiar with the platform and have invested significant time and resources into customizing and integrating it with their workflow. On the other hand, Plane is a good choice for smaller to medium-sized teams who value data ownership and flexibility, and are willing to invest time and technical expertise into setting up and configuring the platform.
Plane is also a good option for teams who are looking for a free and self-hosted solution, and are comfortable with a more DIY approach to project management.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format.
2. Use the Plane import tool to import your data into Plane.
3. Configure Plane to match your team's workflow and customize the platform as needed.
4. Integrate Plane with your existing tools and services, such as Git and development platforms.
5. Test and refine your setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still requires significant technical expertise to set up and configure. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's user interface is not as user-friendly as Jira's, which can make it difficult for non-technical team members to use. However, for teams who value data ownership and flexibility, and are willing to invest time and expertise into setting up and configuring the platform, Plane is a good choice. Teams who should switch to Plane are those who are currently using Jira and are looking for a more cost-effective and customizable solution.

## Who Should Switch
* Small to medium-sized teams who value data ownership and flexibility
* Teams who are currently using Jira and are looking for a more cost-effective solution
* Development teams who are already using Git and other development tools
* Teams who are comfortable with a DIY approach to project management
* Teams who do not require a robust feature set or excellent customer support

## FAQ
### Can I use Plane for free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying any licensing fees. However, you will need to cover the cost of hosting and maintaining your own server.
### Is Plane as user-friendly as Jira?
No, Plane's user interface is not as user-friendly as Jira's, which can make it difficult for non-technical team members to use.
### Can I integrate Plane with my existing tools and services?
Yes, Plane can be integrated with a wide range of tools and services, including Git and development platforms.
### Is Plane suitable for large, complex projects?
No, Plane is not yet suitable for very large or complex projects, as it is still a relatively new platform and may not have all the features and scalability required for such projects.
### Can I migrate my data from Jira to Plane?
Yes, you can export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.

# Trello vs WeKan (2026)

## Overview
Trello and WeKan are project management tools that help teams organize and prioritize tasks. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Trello to WeKan, particularly those looking for a self-hosted solution with more control over their data. The core use case for both tools is task management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more flexibility and data ownership.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Trello offers a free plan with limited features, while WeKan is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: WeKan allows teams to host their data on their own servers, while Trello stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: WeKan requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Trello is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Trello is designed to handle large teams and high traffic, while WeKan's scalability depends on the team's server infrastructure.
* Integration with Google Drive: Trello has a built-in integration with Google Drive, while WeKan requires a third-party plugin.

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |

**Trello:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Integrates well with other Atlassian tools
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Has a large user community and support resources
* Limited customization options
**WeKan:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Highly customizable
* Free to use with no per-user costs
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain

Trello is a good choice for teams that need a simple, easy-to-use project management tool with minimal setup and maintenance. WeKan, on the other hand, is suitable for teams that value data ownership and customization, and have the technical expertise to set up and maintain a self-hosted solution. WeKan is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that WeKan's scalability depends on the team's server infrastructure, which can be a bottleneck for large teams. However, for teams that value data ownership and customization, WeKan is a viable alternative to Trello, and we recommend switching if you have the technical resources to support it.

## Who Should Switch

* Teams that require self-hosting and data ownership for security or compliance reasons

* Teams that need high customization options for their workflow

# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are two popular cloud storage solutions that enable individuals and teams to store, share, and collaborate on files. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from a proprietary cloud storage solution to a self-hosted alternative, with the core use case being file storage and collaboration. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Dropbox charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free to use and self-host.
* Data ownership: Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership of their data, while Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* Setup complexity: Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, while Dropbox is generally easier to use out of the box.
* Scalability: Nextcloud can be scaled to meet the needs of large organizations, while Dropbox has limits on the number of users and storage capacity.
* Integration: Nextcloud has a built-in office suite called Nextcloud Office, while Dropbox integrates with Microsoft Office Online.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $499.50-$829/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,998-$3,316/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Integrates with many third-party apps
* Fast and reliable file syncing
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Nextcloud:**
* Self-hosted and free to use
* Retain full ownership of data
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Integrates with many third-party apps
* Can be complex to set up and configure

## When to Choose Each
Dropbox is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple and easy-to-use cloud storage solution. It's ideal for teams that don't require a high level of control over their data and are willing to pay a monthly fee per user. Nextcloud, on the other hand, is a good choice for large organizations or teams that require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and configuring the solution.

Nextcloud is also a good choice for teams that need a self-hosted solution and are looking to reduce costs. It's ideal for teams that have the technical expertise to set up and configure the solution and are willing to manage their own servers.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Dropbox files using the Dropbox API or a third-party tool like dropbox-export.
2. Set up a Nextcloud server and configure the necessary settings and plugins.
3. Import your exported files into Nextcloud using the Nextcloud web interface or a third-party tool like nextcloud-import.
4. Configure any necessary integrations with third-party apps.
5. Test your Nextcloud setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready solution for most users, offering a high level of control over data and a self-hosted option. However, it may not be the best choice for small teams or individuals who don't require a high level of customization and are willing to pay a monthly fee.

One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching to Nextcloud is that it requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and configure, particularly for large organizations. This can be a barrier to adoption for teams that don't have the necessary resources or expertise.

We recommend switching to Nextcloud for teams that require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and configuring the solution. However, for small teams or individuals who don't require a high level of customization, Dropbox may still be a good choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Large organizations with over 100 users that require a high level of control over their data
* Teams that need a self-hosted solution and are looking to reduce costs
* Developers who need a high level of customization and extensibility
* Teams that require a high level of security and compliance
* Organizations that need to integrate their cloud storage solution with other self-hosted tools

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud for free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free to use and self-host. However, you will need to pay for server costs and any necessary hardware or software.

### Is Nextcloud more secure than Dropbox?
Nextcloud offers a high level of security and control over data, but it's not necessarily more secure than Dropbox. Both solutions have their own security measures in place.

### Can I integrate Nextcloud with other apps?
Yes, Nextcloud has a wide range of integrations with third-party apps, including office suites, productivity tools, and more.

### How do I migrate my files from Dropbox to Nextcloud?
You can export your Dropbox files using the Dropbox API or a third-party tool, and then import them into Nextcloud using the Nextcloud web interface or a third-party tool.

### Is Nextcloud suitable for small teams?
Nextcloud can be suitable for small teams, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and configure than Dropbox. It's worth considering whether the benefits of Nextcloud outweigh the costs and complexity for your team.

title: Linear vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Linear vs Plane

## Overview

Streamlined issue tracker known for speed and keyboard-first design. is a popular proprietary tool in the project-management space. Plane is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Linear costs Free / $8/user/month; Plane is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Linear is Proprietary; Plane is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Plane can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Plane eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Plane has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Linear | Plane |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $8/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Linear

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Plane

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [makeplane/plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) * ~31k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Linear if:** Linear is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Plane if:** Plane is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Linear in its standard export format, review Plane import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Plane is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Linear tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Plane instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Linear, switching to self-hosted Plane will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Linear until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Linear paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Plane free to use?
Yes. Plane is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Linear to Plane?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Linear data, follow the Plane import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Plane get regular updates?
Yes. Plane has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Plane without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Plane development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced May 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Linear](https://linear.app) and [Plane](https://plane.so) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Plane is a free, self-hosted alternative to Linear. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Google Workspace vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Google Workspace vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Google suite of cloud productivity tools including Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Meet, and Calendar. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Nextcloud is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Google Workspace costs $6-$18/user/month; Nextcloud is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Google Workspace is Proprietary; Nextcloud is AGPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: Nextcloud can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Nextcloud eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Nextcloud has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$300/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,200/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Google Workspace

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Google Workspace if:** Google Workspace is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Google Workspace in its standard export format, review Nextcloud import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Google Workspace tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Google Workspace, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Google Workspace until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Google Workspace paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Google Workspace to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Google Workspace data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced May 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Google Workspace](https://workspace.google.com) and [Nextcloud](https://nextcloud.com) before making decisions.*
